title: Acute compartment syndrome

related.why: Why a present pulse can mislead

brief.scenario: A 24-year-old man sustained a closed right tibial shaft fracture 8 hours ago. It was manipulated and placed in a plaster cast. The nurse asks you to review him because his pain has increased markedly over the last 2 hours despite analgesia.
brief.task: Assess the patient and explain your management to the examiner. The examiner will give you findings as you go.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Tibial fracture + pain out of proportion = compartment syndrome until proven otherwise.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: A warm foot with a palpable pulse does not exclude it.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Say "I'm concerned about acute compartment syndrome" in your first sentence.

flow: Respond to prompts: pressures, surgery, complications

grid.label: Recognition
grid.fail: Attributes pain to the fracture; does not consider compartment syndrome.
grid.borderline: Names compartment syndrome only after prompting.
grid.pass: Names compartment syndrome as the concern.
grid.high: Names it immediately and links it to disproportionate, escalating pain after a tibial fracture.

grid.label: Pain assessment
grid.fail: Treats pain with more analgesia only.
grid.borderline: Asks about the pain but does not test passive stretch.
grid.pass: Asks about severity and progression; tests pain on passive stretch.
grid.high: Treats rising analgesic requirement as a warning sign and knows which passive movement stretches which compartment.

grid.label: Neurovascular examination
grid.fail: Relies on pulse; states present pulse excludes the diagnosis.
grid.borderline: Examines neurovascular status but hesitates when told the pulse is present.
grid.pass: Assesses compartments, sensation, motor function and perfusion; states a pulse does not exclude it.
grid.high: Compares all four compartments with the other leg and tests first web space sensation (deep peroneal nerve).

grid.label: Escalation
grid.fail: Plans to review later or does not escalate.
grid.borderline: Plans to escalate, but only after further tests.
grid.pass: Escalates urgently to the on-call orthopaedic team.
grid.high: Calls the orthopaedic registrar and consultant now, and alerts theatres for possible fasciotomy.

grid.label: Immediate limb measures
grid.borderline: Releases the dressings but leaves cast padding in place.
grid.pass: Releases circumferential dressings and cast to expose the skin.
grid.high: Splits cast and padding to skin, elevates the limb, re-evaluates within 30 minutes.

grid.label: Pressure measurement
grid.fail: Waits for pressures before escalating a clear diagnosis.
grid.borderline: Knows pressures are an adjunct but cannot say when to use them.
grid.pass: Uses pressures only when clinical findings are equivocal or assessment is unreliable.
grid.high: Gives delta pressure < 30 mmHg as increased risk; notes the consultant decides; > 40 mmHg: consider urgent decompression.

grid.label: Definitive surgery
grid.borderline: Says 'surgery' but names fasciotomy only when prompted.
grid.pass: States immediate fasciotomy is required once diagnosed.
grid.high: Two-incision four-compartment decompression, debride dead muscle, wounds left open, plastics within 24 h, relook within 72 h.

grid.label: Systemic complications
grid.borderline: Mentions the kidneys only when prompted.
grid.pass: Mentions rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury.
grid.high: Checks CK, potassium, renal function and urine output; plans renal protection.

grid.label: Masked assessment
grid.fail: Is reassured by a nerve block, sedation or improving pain on opioids.
grid.borderline: Says a block makes assessment harder but gives no monitoring plan.
grid.pass: Recognises that blocks, reduced consciousness and opioids make assessment unreliable.
grid.high: Plans hourly documented assessment and considers continuous compartment pressure monitoring.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's probably post-reduction pain. I'd give him more morphine.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: The foot is warm and the pulse is present.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Good, so the circulation is fine and it isn't compartment syndrome.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What would you do about the plaster?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd loosen it a bit and see him again on the ward round.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Yes, I'd get the pressures and wait for the result before calling anyone.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'm concerned about acute compartment syndrome because his pain is increasing despite analgesia.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd ask about severity and progression, test pain on passive stretch, feel the compartments, and check sensation, movement and perfusion. A present pulse wouldn't exclude it.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The leg is tense and passive stretch is very painful. What now?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd escalate urgently to the on-call orthopaedic team and release the cast and dressings down to the skin.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Not if the diagnosis is clear. Only if the findings were equivocal or he couldn't be assessed reliably.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What is the definitive treatment, and what else worries you?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Immediate fasciotomy. I'd also watch for rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: What if he'd had a nerve block?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Then his pain wouldn't be a reliable guide, so I couldn't be reassured by it.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Acute compartment syndrome. Escalating pain out of proportion to a tibial fracture is the key early sign, and his rising analgesic requirement is itself a warning.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd compare all four compartments with the other leg. Passive plantarflexion stretches the anterior compartment, dorsiflexion the posterior ones. I'd test first web space sensation for the deep peroneal nerve. A palpable pulse wouldn't exclude it.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The leg is tense, passive plantarflexion is very painful and the first web space is numb. The pulse is present.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's compartment syndrome. I'd call the orthopaedic registrar and consultant now and alert theatres. Meanwhile I'd split the cast and padding to skin, elevate the limb and re-evaluate within 30 minutes.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Not when the diagnosis is clinically clear. If it were equivocal, I'd measure all suspected compartments with a concurrent blood pressure. A delta pressure under 30 mmHg means increased risk, and the consultant decides whether to decompress. Above 40 mmHg absolute, urgent decompression should be considered.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Immediate two-incision, four-compartment fasciotomy, debriding non-viable muscle. The wounds are left open, with plastic surgery input within 24 hours and a relook within 72 hours.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Rhabdomyolysis. I'd check CK, potassium, renal function and urine output and protect the kidneys. And if he'd had a nerve block or was sedated, I'd do hourly documented assessments and consider continuous pressure monitoring.

failures.move: Being reassured by a warm foot and palpable pulse.
failures.consequence: Pulses are often preserved; the diagnosis is missed at the stage when it is treatable.

failures.move: Waiting for pressure readings before escalating a clear clinical picture.
failures.consequence: Delays fasciotomy while the muscle is still salvageable.

failures.move: Stopping at 'surgery' without saying what the operation is.
failures.consequence: Leaves nothing to say when the examiner asks what the operation involves.

failures.move: Forgetting the kidneys when asked 'anything else?'
failures.consequence: Misses the systemic complication that can kill the patient after the limb is saved.

failures.move: Accepting improved pain after morphine or a block as reassurance.
failures.consequence: Masked symptoms delay diagnosis — a recognised pattern in missed cases.

recovery.line: I'd measure all suspected compartments with a concurrent blood pressure and interpret them with my consultant.

recovery.when: The examiner says the pain has improved
recovery.line: That doesn't reassure me — the rising analgesic requirement is itself a warning sign.

knowledge.fact: Lower leg compartments: anterior, lateral, superficial posterior, deep posterior.
Passive stretch: plantarflexion → anterior; inversion → lateral; dorsiflexion → posterior compartments.
First dorsal web space numbness = deep peroneal nerve, which runs in the anterior compartment.
Delta pressure = diastolic BP − compartment pressure; < 30 mmHg indicates increased risk.
After a tibial fracture, stay alert for compartment syndrome for 48 hours after injury or fixation.
Late presentation: decision involves two consultants; non-operative management with renal protection is an option.

recall.think: Muscle and nerve death within hours; limb and kidneys at risk.
do: Split cast and padding to skin, elevate

sources.name: BOA Standard: Diagnosis and Management of Compartment Syndrome of the Extremities
sources.supports: Hourly assessment, release to skin and elevation, 30-minute re-evaluation, pressure thresholds, consultant decision, fasciotomy technique, plastics and relook timing, late presentation

sources.name: NICE NG37: Fractures (complex): assessment and management
sources.supports: 48-hour awareness after tibial fracture; continuous pressure monitoring when the patient is unconscious or has a nerve block

partner.opening: Please assess this patient's leg and tell me what you're concerned about. I'll give you findings as you go.

reveals.finding: Pain 9/10, worse over 2 hours, needed two extra morphine doses.
Calf and anterior leg swollen and tense compared with the left.
Severe pain on passive plantarflexion of the ankle and toes.
Reduced sensation in the first dorsal web space.
Foot warm, capillary refill 2 seconds, dorsalis pedis palpable.

push.question: Who would you call, and how quickly?
push.expect: Orthopaedic registrar and consultant now; theatres alerted.

push.question: What exactly would you do with the plaster?
push.expect: Split cast and padding to skin, elevate, re-evaluate in 30 min.

push.question: Diastolic 80, compartment 55. Interpret.
push.expect: ΔP 25 mmHg — below 30, increased risk; consultant decides.

push.question: Describe the operation.
push.expect: Two-incision, four-compartment fasciotomy; wounds left open.

push.question: What systemic problem worries you?
push.expect: Rhabdomyolysis: CK, potassium, renal function, urine output.

curveballs.prompt: His pain is better after morphine. Are you reassured?
curveballs.safeAnswer: No — rising analgesic need is a warning sign; reassess objectively.

curveballs.prompt: The foot is pink with a strong pulse.

curveballs.safeAnswer: Severe escalating pain after a tibial fracture needs objective assessment, not dismissal.

curveballs.prompt: He presents 36 hours late with an insensate, firm leg.
curveballs.safeAnswer: High surgical risk; decision involves two consultants; non-operative management with renal protection is an option.
